The word "prohibitive" describes something that acts as a practical stopper — a barrier so extreme that it either outright forbids you from doing something, or makes doing it so unrealistic that almost nobody can proceed.

Think of it like an invisible wall. Technically, you might not be legally stopped from doing something, but the obstacle in front of you is so enormous — usually the cost, but sometimes the effort, complexity, or risk — that the wall might as well be real.

Meaning 1 — So extreme that it stops you (the dominant, everyday use)

When most people use "prohibitive," this is what they mean. A cost, price, fee, or effort is so high or so intense that it effectively rules out the option for most ordinary people.

Nothing illegal is happening. Nobody is technically forbidden. But the barrier is so crushing that the realistic answer for most people is: I simply cannot do this.

Imagine you want to buy a house in a major city, but the prices are $5 million for the smallest apartment. Nothing stops you from buying — but the price is prohibitive. It shuts the door on most people, even if the door isn't locked.

More examples:

  • "The cost of the medical treatment was prohibitive for families without insurance." — So expensive that most families couldn't access it.
  • "The repair bill was prohibitive, so she bought a new phone instead." — Repairing it would cost so much it made no sense.
  • "The entrance requirements for that university are prohibitive for most applicants." — The requirements are so intense and demanding that most people can't realistically meet them.

A crucial nuance: "Prohibitive" does not simply mean "expensive" or "difficult." Plenty of things are expensive or difficult without being prohibitive. The word implies a specific threshold — so extreme that it stops you. A $200 restaurant meal is expensive. A $20,000 restaurant meal is prohibitive.

Meaning 2 — Serving to legally forbid something (the more formal use)

In legal, governmental, or formal contexts, "prohibitive" can describe a law, rule, or regulation that outright bans something. This is the more literal use of the word, where the stopping force is a rule rather than a cost.

  • "The government introduced prohibitive measures against the dumping of waste in rivers." — Laws specifically designed to ban this activity.
  • "Prohibitive tariffs on imported goods made foreign products nearly impossible to sell here." — Trade taxes so high they effectively ban foreign competition. (A "prohibitive tariff" is a common phrase in economics for exactly this.)
  • "Prohibitive zoning laws prevented any new construction in the area." — Regulations that forbid building.

You will very commonly see this word as the adverb "prohibitively," placed before another adjective to mean "to a degree that blocks you."

  • "Prohibitively expensive" — the single most common phrase you'll encounter
  • "Prohibitively complex"
  • "Prohibitively risky"
  • "Prohibitively time-consuming"

When someone says a treatment is prohibitively expensive, they don't just mean it costs a lot. They mean the expense is at a level that makes the option functionally off the table.

In sports, betting, and competitive contexts, you'll sometimes hear the phrase "prohibitive favorite." This describes a competitor who is so overwhelmingly expected to win that backing anyone else seems almost irrational.

  • "The reigning champion entered the tournament as a prohibitive favorite."

The idea is that the gap between the favorite and everyone else is so wide, it "prohibits" any sensible expectation of an upset.

These two words are closely related but mean different things, and it's worth being clear on the distinction.

Prohibited means something is actually forbidden — by a rule, a law, or an authority. The action is not allowed. "Smoking is prohibited in this building."

Prohibitive describes something that acts like a prohibition — either by being so costly or extreme that it stops you (Meaning 1), or by being a formal rule that forbids something (Meaning 2).

The sharpest way to feel the difference: alcohol might be prohibited in a dry county (it's banned). But in a luxury hotel bar, the price of a whisky might be prohibitive (it's not banned — it's just $80 a glass and you're walking away). In the first case, a law stops you. In the second, the cost does.

"Prohibitive" as an adjective describes something that functions as a stopper or wall — either because a cost, effort, or barrier is so extreme that it makes something practically impossible for most people, or because a law or rule outright forbids it. The dominant, everyday use is almost always about cost or effort being unreasonably extreme. The word always carries the sense of: not just hard — hard enough to stop you.
